title: GOD HATES DIVORCE… BUT DOES THAT MEAN HE WANTS YOU TO STAY AND BE DESTROYED?
paragraphs: GOD HATES DIVORCE… BUT DOES THAT MEAN HE WANTS YOU TO STAY AND BE DESTROYED?
When the Marriage You Prayed For Becomes the Place You Fear Most — What Scripture Really Says About Abuse, Covenant, Separation, and the God Who Sees Your Tears
There is a woman reading this who knows exactly how to recognize footsteps.
Not because she is excited that her husband is home.
But because she has learned to tell, by the sound of his shoes against the floor, whether tonight will be peaceful… or whether she needs to prepare herself for another storm.
She knows which questions not to ask.
Which subjects not to mention.
How to smile when something inside her is collapsing.

She knows how to wipe away tears before the children notice. How to cover a bruise with clothing. How to apologize for something she never did, simply because an apology might end the argument faster.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part?
She still prays for him.
She still believes God can change him.
She still remembers the man who once stood before an altar and promised to love her.
But somewhere between the wedding vows and the sleepless nights, a terrible question began haunting her.
“If I leave to protect myself, am I disobeying God?”
Maybe you are that woman.
Maybe you are a husband who has endured years of humiliation, intimidation, manipulation, or violence behind closed doors.
Maybe you grew up watching your mother suffer while people from church kept telling her to pray harder.
Or maybe you are the pastor, friend, parent, or Christian who once told someone to stay without understanding what was happening when nobody else was watching.
Whatever brought you here, please don't rush past this.
Because there is something we desperately need to confront.
What happens when the very Scriptures meant to reveal God's heart are used to convince a wounded person that God requires their continued destruction?
And what if some of the words you have heard about marriage are biblical in themselves, but have been applied in ways that betray the very character of the God who spoke them?
This is not an article celebrating divorce.
This is not an attack on marriage.
This is not permission to abandon a covenant whenever love becomes difficult.
This is a conversation about something far more serious.
The difference between suffering for righteousness and suffering under another person's unrepentant cruelty.
The difference between covenant faithfulness and coercive control.
The difference between forgiveness and access.
And the difference between a marriage that is wounded but willing to heal… and a marriage in which one person is using fear to dominate the other.
Because Jesus Christ did not come to teach the powerful how to use religion to keep the vulnerable silent.
He came to reveal the Father.
And the Father's heart matters.
More than our traditions.
More than our reputations.
More than the appearance of a perfect Christian family.
Even more than the comfortable answers we have repeated without examining what Scripture actually says.
There is a sentence many Christians know.
“God hates divorce.”
It is often spoken with certainty.
Sometimes with compassion.
Sometimes with devastating carelessness.
The words are associated with Malachi 2:16, and they deserve careful examination.
The Hebrew text of Malachi 2:16 is difficult, and its wording has been translated differently across Bible versions.
One significant phrase in the passage is:
כִּי־שָׂנֵא שַׁלַּח
Ki sane shallach.

The words concern hatred and sending away, or divorce, but the grammatical relationship is disputed. Some translations understand the statement as God expressing hatred of divorce. Others render it as a condemnation of a man who hates and divorces his wife.
This is not a trivial distinction.
And here is something even more important.
Read the surrounding passage.
Malachi 2:14 identifies the wife as a man's companion and the wife of his covenant.
Malachi 2:16 also condemns violence or wrongdoing, expressed in the Hebrew image of covering one's garment with violence.
The Hebrew word חָמָס — chamas means violence, wrongdoing, or injustice.
The passage is not a divine invitation for abusive spouses to terrorize their partners while hiding behind the permanence of marriage.
It is a prophetic confrontation of covenant treachery.
God is confronting faithlessness.
God is confronting injustice.
God is confronting those who violate the covenant they were supposed to honor.
Think about that.
A passage sometimes used to silence wounded spouses is actually part of a prophetic rebuke against those who deal treacherously with them.
That should make us tremble before using it carelessly.
Because when we take a verse out of its context, we can turn a warning to the oppressor into a burden placed upon the oppressed.
And that is a dangerous thing to do with the Word of God.
Now consider another passage.
Ephesians 5.
Perhaps you have heard someone quote Ephesians 5:22, which instructs wives to submit to their husbands.
But have you noticed how frequently the conversation stops there?
How often the responsibilities of the husband are reduced to a few pleasant words, while the responsibilities of the wife are treated as unconditional?
Paul does not present Christian marriage as a license for male domination.
Ephesians 5:21 speaks of believers submitting to one another in reverence for Christ.
Then Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
The Greek expression is:
ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας
Agapate tas gynaikas.
“Love your wives.”
The verb comes from ἀγαπάω — agapaō, meaning to love.
And Paul does not leave the nature of that love undefined.
He points directly to Jesus Christ.
A husband is commanded to love in a manner shaped by Christ's self-giving sacrifice.
Not by intimidation.
Not by humiliation.
Not by threats.
Not by demanding unquestioning obedience.
Not by treating his wife's fear as evidence of his authority.
Jesus laid down His life for His bride. He did not demand that His bride be destroyed to protect His ego.
Read that again.
The cross reveals sacrificial love, not sanctified cruelty.
Colossians 3:19 reinforces this responsibility.
The Greek text says:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας καὶ μὴ πικραίνεσθε πρὸς αὐτάς.
Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas kai mē pikrainesthe pros autas.
“Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them.”
The verb πικραίνω — pikrainō can convey bitterness or embittering treatment.
Paul explicitly rejects the harshness that can poison the marriage relationship.
So ask yourself something.
If Scripture commands a husband not to treat his wife harshly, how can someone use that same Scripture to excuse his cruelty?
If Christlike leadership requires sacrificial love, how can intimidation be presented as spiritual leadership?
If marriage is supposed to reflect the relationship between Christ and His church, how can a home governed by terror be celebrated as a model of biblical marriage?
It cannot.
Not without distorting the picture.
Not without misrepresenting Jesus.
And not without harming the people God calls us to protect.
But perhaps you are thinking about another passage.
Jesus said that what God has joined together, no one should separate.
Yes.
He did.
In Matthew 19:6, Jesus defends the seriousness of marriage and warns against treating covenant commitments casually.
His words deserve our obedience, not our dismissal.
But we must also remember the conversation in which He spoke them.
Jesus was answering a question about whether a man could divorce his wife for virtually any reason.
In that cultural setting, divorce could leave a woman vulnerable and without meaningful protection.
Jesus confronted the hardheartedness that permitted men to discard their wives.
He was not giving abusive spouses permission to imprison their partners in danger.
And yet, this is where careful interpretation matters.

Jesus' teaching establishes a high view of marriage. It does not explicitly answer every modern question about domestic violence, temporary separation, protective orders, or the civil dissolution of an abusive marriage.
Christians who faithfully honor Scripture disagree about some of those applications.
We must not pretend otherwise.
Some Christian traditions recognize abuse, abandonment, or serious covenant violation as grounds that may justify divorce.
Others permit protective separation while maintaining more restrictive teachings about divorce and remarriage.
Those differences are real.
But here is a moral distinction we must never erase.
A person can take immediate steps to escape danger without first settling every theological question about divorce and remarriage.
Safety is not the enemy of covenant faithfulness.
Seeking protection is not the same as despising marriage.
And refusing to remain available for violence is not the same as refusing to trust God.
There is another verse that deserves our attention.
First Corinthians 7:10–11.
Paul instructs married believers not to separate, while also acknowledging the possibility that a wife has separated from her husband.
His instruction is that she remain unmarried or be reconciled, and that a husband not divorce his wife.
This passage must not be ignored.
It is part of the biblical witness.
But neither should it be treated as though Paul were commanding a woman being beaten, threatened, or sexually assaulted to return immediately to the person harming her.
The passage does not specifically address the full range of abusive situations.
Its application requires wisdom, pastoral care, and attention to the whole counsel of Scripture.
Paul also speaks in First Corinthians 7:15 about a believer not being enslaved when an unbelieving spouse departs, adding that God has called believers to peace.
The Greek phrase is:
ἐν δὲ εἰρήνῃ κέκληκεν ἡμᾶς ὁ θεός
En de eirēnē keklēken hēmas ho theos.
“God has called us to peace.”
In context, Paul is discussing abandonment by an unbelieving spouse. We should not pretend that the verse directly establishes every possible ground for divorce.
Nevertheless, it reminds us that peace is not irrelevant to Christian marriage.
And peace does not mean maintaining appearances while terror reigns behind the front door.
Biblical peace is not merely the absence of public arguments.
It is not the silence of someone too frightened to speak.
It is not the fragile calm that follows a threat.
Sometimes what appears peaceful to outsiders is actually a household in which one person has learned to disappear emotionally to survive.
And that is not the peace of Christ.
Perhaps the most painful misunderstanding comes from the way Christians sometimes speak about suffering.
“Carry your cross.”
“Turn the other cheek.”
“Forgive seventy times seven.”
“Love your enemies.”
These are the words of Jesus.
Precious words.
Holy words.
Words that confront our selfishness, revenge, pride, and hatred.
But they must be understood as Jesus intended.
When Jesus calls His disciples to take up their cross, He calls them to faithful allegiance to Him, even when that allegiance brings suffering.
He does not command people to cooperate with someone else's sin.
When Jesus teaches us to turn the other cheek, He forbids personal retaliation. That teaching must not be turned into a rule requiring someone to remain physically accessible to repeated assault.
When Jesus commands forgiveness, He calls us away from vengeance and bitterness.
He does not teach that forgiveness eliminates accountability.
And when Jesus commands love for enemies, He does not require us to hand those enemies unlimited opportunities to harm us.
Consider Jesus Himself.
In John 18:22–23, an officer strikes Him.
Jesus does not respond with violent revenge.
But He does challenge the injustice.
He asks why He was struck if He spoke rightly.
The sinless Son of God did not treat an unjust blow as morally acceptable.
And in Matthew 10:23, Jesus instructs His disciples that when they are persecuted in one town, they may flee to another.
Flight from danger is not automatically cowardice.
Sometimes it is wisdom.
Proverbs 22:3 teaches that the prudent recognize danger and take refuge, while the inexperienced continue and suffer.
The Hebrew word עָרוּם — arum in this context refers to the prudent or shrewd person.
Recognizing danger is not necessarily a failure of faith.
It can be an expression of discernment.

So if you are living with someone who threatens your life, strikes you, coerces you sexually, controls your movement, isolates you from family, or uses fear to control your decisions, please hear this carefully.
You do not need to prove your faith by remaining within reach of the next assault.
That is not a rejection of the cross.
It is a refusal to confuse another person's sin with God's will for your life.
And there is something else we need to talk about.
Abuse does not always leave bruises.
Sometimes it leaves a person questioning their own memory.

Sometimes it looks like a spouse who monitors every conversation, controls every peso or dollar, humiliates you privately, threatens to take the children, or makes you feel guilty for having ordinary human needs.
Sometimes it is spiritual.
A husband quotes Scripture to silence his wife.
A wife uses threats, manipulation, and humiliation to control her husband.
A partner declares that disagreeing with them is the same as rebelling against God.
Someone says, “If you were a real Christian, you would forgive me and stop bringing this up.”
But they have not confessed honestly.
They have not accepted responsibility.
They have not stopped the behavior.
They simply want the consequences to disappear.
This is not biblical repentance.
Second Corinthians 7:10–11 describes godly sorrow as producing repentance and a seriousness about putting wrong right.
True repentance is more than tears.
More than promises.
More than a dramatic apology after another terrifying night.
More than a sudden interest in church because a spouse is preparing to leave.
Genuine repentance includes truthful acknowledgment of wrongdoing, rejection of excuses, willingness to face consequences, and observable change over time.
And even then, a person who has been abused is not obligated to resume living together before safety has been established.
A sincere apology does not instantly rebuild shattered trust.
A prayer does not automatically remove the need for professional intervention.
A conversion testimony does not replace accountability.
And forgiveness is not the same as reconciliation.
Forgiveness can be extended without restoring access.
Reconciliation requires truth, safety, responsibility, and genuine change.
Trust must be rebuilt.
It cannot be demanded.
There is a difference between a sinner who is broken over the harm they caused and a manipulator who is angry that their victim finally established boundaries.
One seeks transformation.
The other seeks control.
And we must learn to recognize the difference.
Perhaps you have been waiting for God to change your spouse.
Years have passed.
You have prayed through sleepless nights.
You have fasted.
You have attended marriage seminars.
You have memorized Scriptures.
You have told yourself that if you become quieter, kinder, more submissive, more patient, more spiritual, perhaps everything will finally become peaceful.
But the violence continues.
The threats continue.
The humiliation continues.
And now you are wondering whether God is disappointed in you because you are exhausted.
Listen carefully.
God sees what happens when the church service ends.
He sees what happens after the smiling family photograph.
He sees the trembling hands.
The messages you are afraid to answer.
The children who freeze when someone raises their voice.
The prayers whispered into pillows.
The fear you have learned to call normal.
Psalm 34:18 declares:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.” — KJV
The Hebrew expression for the brokenhearted is:
נִשְׁבְּרֵי־לֵב — nishberei-lev
Those whose hearts are broken or crushed.
The psalm does not portray God as indifferent to shattered people.
It presents Him as near.
Near to the heart that has been broken.
Near to the person who has no strength left to explain.
Near to those whose suffering has been dismissed by people who should have listened.
And if you are the one who has been harmed, I want you to consider a woman in Scripture.
Hagar.
She was vulnerable.
She was mistreated.
She fled into the wilderness.
Genesis 16 tells us that the angel of the LORD found her there.
And in Genesis 16:13, she gave a name to the God who had spoken to her.
אֵל רֳאִי — El Roi.
Commonly understood as “God who sees me,” though the precise Hebrew expression has interpretive complexities.
What an extraordinary moment.
A woman who had been treated as disposable discovered that she was not invisible to God.
Now, we must handle her story honestly.
In that first encounter, Hagar was instructed to return to Sarai. That difficult detail is in Scripture, and it should not be concealed.
But neither should that specific command, given within Hagar's unique historical circumstances, be turned into a universal instruction for abused spouses to return to dangerous homes.
Later, in Genesis 21, Hagar again finds herself in the wilderness, and God hears the cry of her son and provides for them.
Her story is not a simple formula for every marriage crisis.
It is a testimony that God sees people whom others overlook.
And perhaps that is what you most need to hear.
You have not been forgotten.
You are not invisible.
The fact that others have misunderstood your suffering does not mean God has misunderstood it.
The fact that someone has used His name to control you does not mean that person represents His heart.
And the fact that you are frightened does not make you spiritually inferior.
There is another group of people who need to hear this message.
The children.
The little boy who lies awake listening for shouting.
The little girl who has learned to recognize the sound of something breaking.
The teenager who quietly believes that love means enduring humiliation.
The child who watches one parent abuse the other and begins to assume that this is what marriage looks like.
We often speak about preserving the family.
And family matters deeply.
But preserving the appearance of a family while children are exposed to violence is not the same as protecting the family.
Children need more than two parents living under one roof.
They need safety.
They need stability.
They need examples of truth, dignity, repentance, and love.
They need to learn that cruelty is not authority.
That fear is not respect.
That control is not intimacy.
That saying “I love you” does not cancel out violence.
And that the name of Jesus must never be used to justify terror.
Ephesians 6:4 warns fathers against provoking their children to wrath and calls them to raise children in the instruction of the Lord.
A home where children live in chronic fear contradicts the spirit of that calling.
We should never casually tell a parent to remain in a dangerous environment “for the children” without considering what those children are experiencing.
Sometimes protecting the children requires protecting the parent who is being harmed.
And sometimes that means leaving a dangerous home.
Not necessarily making an immediate final decision about divorce.
Not necessarily knowing what the next ten years will look like.
But taking the next necessary step toward safety.

If this is your situation, do not announce a departure or confront an abusive partner in a way that could increase danger. Separation can be a particularly dangerous time. When possible, make a confidential safety plan with a qualified domestic violence advocate, and involve emergency services when immediate danger exists.
Use a safe device if your communications are monitored.
Preserve evidence only when it is safe and lawful to do so.
Seek appropriate medical attention for injuries.
Get independent legal advice about protection, custody, finances, and separation.

And please understand that ordinary couples counseling can be unsafe when one partner is using intimidation or coercive control. Specialized assessment and individual support may be needed before any joint intervention is considered.
There is no shame in asking for help.
There is no shame in seeking protection.
And there is no shame in admitting that the situation is more serious than you once wanted to believe.
Now, I need to speak to the person who has been causing the harm.
Perhaps you are reading this and feeling angry.
Perhaps you are preparing to explain why your spouse provoked you.
Perhaps you are telling yourself that you only shouted because they would not listen.
That you only threatened them because you were afraid of losing them.
That you only pushed them because you lost control.
That you only monitored their phone because you loved them.
Stop.
Your spouse's imperfections do not justify your cruelty.
Your anger does not excuse violence.
Your jealousy does not excuse surveillance and control.
Your position in the household does not make you the owner of another human being.
And your knowledge of Scripture does not make you spiritually mature if you are using it to frighten someone into submission.
James 1:20 says:
“For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.” — KJV
You cannot build a Christ-centered marriage through fear.
You cannot claim to represent Jesus while refusing to take responsibility for the harm you inflict.
And you cannot demand forgiveness as a shortcut around repentance.
If you have abused your spouse, the faithful response is not to pressure them to return.
It is to stop the abuse, respect their boundaries, accept accountability, and seek qualified, specialized help.
Do not ask them to manage your emotions.
Do not make your repentance dependent on whether they reconcile.
Do not use your children, pastor, relatives, or congregation to pressure them.
And do not confuse being sorry about consequences with being broken over sin.
The Gospel offers forgiveness to sinners.
But grace is not permission to continue harming people.
Jesus does not merely excuse sin.
He calls sinners to repentance and new life.
Remember Zacchaeus in Luke 19.
When salvation entered his house, his response included concrete restitution for wrongdoing.
His transformation did not remain a private feeling.
It affected the people he had harmed.
That is what repentance does.
It moves beyond words.
It begins bearing fruit.
And if you truly want to honor Christ, you must be willing to face the truth even when it costs you comfort, control, reputation, or the outcome you desire.
Now let me speak to the church.
Because sometimes the deepest wound does not come only from the abusive spouse.
Sometimes it comes from the people who were supposed to help.
The pastor who refused to listen.
The ministry leader who insisted that the couple pray together despite credible threats.
The friend who told the victim that exposing the abuse would damage the church's reputation.
The relative who said that enduring violence was simply part of being a good Christian wife.
The congregation that welcomed the abuser's public testimony while quietly questioning the victim's character.
Brothers and sisters, this must grieve us.
Isaiah 1:17 commands God's people to learn to do good, seek justice, correct oppression, and defend the vulnerable.
The Hebrew imperative דִּרְשׁוּ מִשְׁפָּט — dirshu mishpat means “seek justice.”
Justice is not an optional decoration attached to biblical faith.
It is part of God's moral concern.
Micah 6:8 likewise calls God's people to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with Him.
Mercy without truth can become enabling.
Forgiveness without accountability can become a shield for ongoing wrongdoing.
And an obsession with protecting the institution of marriage, while ignoring the person being harmed, can become a tragic inversion of Christian priorities.
Church leaders should take disclosures of abuse seriously.
They should not automatically require victims to confront their abusers.
They should not promise confidentiality when safeguarding or legal reporting obligations require action.
They should not treat abuse as merely a communication problem between equally responsible spouses.
They should involve qualified professionals and follow applicable safeguarding laws.
They should remember that their responsibility is not merely to preserve a wedding photograph.
It is to shepherd human beings made in the image of God.
A church should be a place where truth can be spoken without terror.
Where the wounded can ask for help without being shamed.
Where repentance is taken seriously.
Where the vulnerable are protected.
And where Jesus Christ is honored not only by the sermons preached, but by the people defended.
Perhaps you are asking the hardest question of all.
“But what about the vow?”
You stood before God.
You promised for better or worse.
In sickness and in health.
Until death.
Doesn't that mean you must endure anything?
Marriage vows are serious.
They should never be treated lightly.
But “for better or worse” is not a promise to facilitate another person's violence.
It is a promise of covenant faithfulness through the ordinary and extraordinary hardships of life.
It is not a divine authorization for one spouse to terrorize the other.
An abusive spouse is not honoring the covenant simply because they refuse to sign divorce papers.
Remaining legally married is not, by itself, evidence of covenant faithfulness.
A person can violate the moral substance of a marriage while insisting upon its legal permanence.
And this is where Christians must be both courageous and humble.
The Bible clearly condemns violence, oppression, cruelty, and covenant treachery.
It clearly honors marriage.
It clearly calls believers to forgiveness and repentance.
But it does not provide one simple, universally agreed-upon sentence resolving every modern question about whether particular forms of abuse establish biblical grounds for divorce and remarriage.
We should not manufacture certainty where careful Christian interpreters disagree.
For some, the question of divorce will involve prolonged prayer, trusted pastoral counsel, legal advice, and examination of their church's doctrinal teaching.
For others, the severity of the danger will require immediate protective action.
Both situations deserve serious care.
And no one should be pressured to risk their life while a theological debate continues.
Because the question is not whether marriage matters.
It does.
The question is whether God requires a person to remain exposed to violence in order to demonstrate that marriage matters.
Scripture does not establish such a requirement.
And we must not add one in God's name.
But perhaps your situation is different.
There has been no physical assault.
No direct threat.
Yet you feel yourself disappearing.
Every conversation becomes an accusation.
Every attempt to explain your pain is twisted into evidence that you are ungrateful, rebellious, or spiritually defective.
You have lost friendships.
You are afraid to express an opinion.
You feel responsible for preventing every emotional explosion.
You are constantly apologizing.
And you no longer know whether what you are experiencing is abuse or simply a difficult marriage.
Please do not dismiss that confusion.
Not every painful disagreement is abuse.
Not every angry argument establishes a pattern of coercive control.
Marriage can involve serious conflict without one spouse systematically dominating the other.
But a persistent pattern of threats, degradation, isolation, intimidation, surveillance, financial restriction, sexual coercion, or punishment for independence deserves serious attention.
You do not need to wait for a visible injury before seeking a confidential assessment from someone trained to recognize domestic abuse.
And you do not need to convince the entire church that your suffering is legitimate before you are allowed to ask for help.
There is something profoundly revealing about the ministry of Jesus.
Again and again, He moved toward people whom respectable society preferred to overlook.
The sick.
The shamed.
The grieving.
The excluded.
The morally compromised.
The spiritually exhausted.
He did not tell the wounded that their pain was inconvenient to His mission.
He saw them.
He listened.
He called people to truth.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He offered mercy without pretending that sin was harmless.
And ultimately, He carried our sin to the cross.
Not because evil was acceptable.
But because evil was so serious that redemption required the sacrifice of the Son of God.
This is why the Gospel must remain at the center of this conversation.
Not merely our emotional reactions.
Not merely our preferred church traditions.
Not merely our experiences, however painful.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified and risen.
Full of grace and truth.
The Savior who forgives sinners and calls them to repentance.
The Lord who cares for the oppressed and commands His people to love their neighbors.
The Redeemer who can transform lives without requiring us to deny reality.
There are marriages in which genuine repentance, professional intervention, accountability, and sustained change can make restoration possible.
And we should rejoice when that happens.
But we must not make restoration a demand placed upon the person who has been harmed.
We must not confuse hope with denial.
We must not insist that a victim remain in danger to prove that God is capable of miracles.
God's power is not diminished when someone seeks safety.
And a testimony does not become less holy because its ending is different from what the church expected.
Sometimes the testimony is a marriage genuinely restored through repentance and grace.
Sometimes it is a person finding safety after years of fear.
Sometimes it is children finally sleeping peacefully.
Sometimes it is an abuser accepting responsibility without demanding reconciliation.
Sometimes it is a wounded believer rediscovering the character of Jesus after years of hearing His name misused.
And sometimes the miracle begins with one quiet sentence.
“I need help.”
That sentence may not sound dramatic.
It may be whispered through tears.
It may be typed with trembling fingers.
It may be spoken to a friend, a counselor, an advocate, or a trusted pastor.
But it can be the beginning of a very different future.
Not necessarily an easy one.
Not one without grief.
Not one without complicated decisions.
But one in which fear no longer has the final word.
And if you are reading this from a place of deep exhaustion, I want to leave you with something.
You are not required to have every answer today.
You do not have to decide the rest of your life before asking for protection.
You do not have to pretend that you are strong.
You do not have to turn your suffering into a public testimony before you have had time to heal.
You are allowed to grieve what you hoped your marriage would become.
You are allowed to love someone and recognize that they are dangerous.
You are allowed to pray for their repentance without making yourself available for further harm.
You are allowed to seek wisdom.
You are allowed to seek help.
And you are allowed to remember that your identity is not exhausted by your marital status.
Your deepest identity, if you belong to Christ, is found in Him.
Not in being the perfect wife.
Not in being the perfect husband.
Not in convincing others that your family is untouched by suffering.
But in being a person whom Jesus Christ has called to Himself.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
This does not erase the complexity of marriage, separation, or divorce.
It does not mean every decision we make is automatically right.
It means our hope rests in Christ rather than in the illusion that we can earn God's acceptance by maintaining a flawless outward appearance.
Grace does not eliminate the need for wisdom.
It gives us a reason to seek truth without despair.
And truth matters even when it disrupts the story we wanted to tell.
Perhaps someone once told you that leaving an abusive marriage would ruin your testimony.
But what if your testimony was never supposed to be about preserving an image?
What if it was supposed to be about discovering that Jesus is still Lord when everything familiar falls apart?
What if the story you are afraid to tell becomes the very story through which another wounded person finally finds courage to ask for help?
Not because pain is glamorous.
Not because divorce is the goal.
Not because suffering should be exploited for attention.
But because the light of Christ reaches places where shame has kept people silent.
And sometimes one person's honest testimony opens a door for someone else.
That is why this message matters beyond the person reading it.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list may be a woman who smiles every Sunday while quietly fearing Monday night.
Somewhere there may be a man who has never told anyone that he is being abused because he believes nobody will take him seriously.
Somewhere there may be an adult child still carrying the wounds of watching violence at home.
Somewhere there may be a pastor who sincerely wants to help but has never been taught how to respond safely.
Not to shame someone publicly.
Not to reveal a survivor's private situation.
But because a message grounded in truth, compassion, and the Gospel might reach someone who has been too frightened to ask the question aloud.
And if tagging someone could expose their situation or increase their danger, send the article privately only through a safe channel, or simply pray for them without identifying them.
Not every passage will be easy to remember in a moment of fear or confusion.
You may need to return to these Scriptures.
You may need to revisit the distinction between forgiveness and reconciliation.
You may need to remind yourself that protecting a person and honoring marriage are not necessarily opposing commitments.
And perhaps someone else will need these words months from now.
If this message has touched something personal, the comments can become a place of encouragement, but never a place where you feel pressured to reveal abuse publicly.
If you have experienced abuse, you owe nobody your story, your location, or the details of your marriage. Your safety and privacy matter more than any public response.

And if you are someone whose marriage has been transformed through genuine repentance, accountability, and Christ-centered change, your testimony may encourage others when shared with wisdom and respect for everyone involved.
Because we need both truth and hope.
We need to tell the truth about abuse.
And we need to tell the truth about the power of Jesus Christ to redeem sinners.
At Gospel Warrior, that is the mission we want to continue pursuing.
Not a Christianity of appearances.
Not a faith that silences difficult questions.
Not content that merely produces an emotional reaction and then leaves people without Scripture.
But ongoing biblical encouragement, careful teaching, discipleship, and resources that help people grow in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
There are people who need more than a passing inspirational quote.
They need to understand the Gospel.
They need to learn how to read Scripture in context.
They need to encounter the mercy and holiness of Jesus.
They need encouragement to repent, forgive, heal, seek wisdom, and walk faithfully with God.
And that work requires time, effort, and resources.
We want those resources to remain a blessing to readers who may not be able to afford books or paid discipleship materials.
For those who prayerfully choose to give, that support can be part of a broader life of Christian generosity and stewardship.
But let us be clear about something important.
The New Testament teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and not coerced.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
The Greek expression μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης — mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs conveys giving neither out of grief or reluctance nor out of compulsion.
That matters deeply.
Supporting Gospel work can glorify God.
Sharing sound biblical teaching can serve others.
Giving generously can be an expression of worship.
God does not sell His grace.
The Gospel is not behind a paywall.
And your value in Christ is not measured by whether you can afford a monthly contribution.
It is the opportunity to help make more Christ-centered resources available to people who need encouragement, sound teaching, and hope.
Pray for the people it may reach.
Help someone find reliable biblical resources.
Encourage a hurting friend to seek appropriate help.
Support your local church's faithful ministry to vulnerable people.
And keep pointing others toward Jesus.
Because the mission is never to make people dependent on Gospel Warrior.
The mission is to help people become more deeply rooted in Christ.
That is what lasting discipleship is about.
Not building admiration for a page.
But directing hearts toward the Savior.
Not making people afraid to ask questions.
But helping them seek answers faithfully.
Not using guilt to raise support.
But inviting willing partners to participate in work they believe honors God.
And not pretending that every Christian story has a simple ending.
But proclaiming that no life is beyond the reach of Christ's grace.
Before we close, I want to return to the person who was there at the beginning.
The one listening for footsteps.
The one hiding tears.
The one wondering whether God is angry because the thought of another night feels unbearable.
I cannot tell you from a distance exactly what legal or marital decision you should make.
I cannot promise that your spouse will change.
I cannot promise that leaving will be simple.
I cannot promise that every church leader or family member will understand.
But I can tell you this.
God's Word does not require you to call evil good.
It does not require you to confuse domination with love.
It does not require you to deny violence to protect someone's reputation.
And it does not require you to remain in immediate danger while waiting for someone else to decide whether your suffering is serious enough.
Jesus Christ is not honored when His name is used as a weapon against the vulnerable.
He is honored when we speak truthfully, love faithfully, pursue justice, practice mercy, and protect those at risk.
The same Jesus who called sinners to repentance also welcomed the weary and burdened.
The same Savior who upheld the seriousness of marriage also condemned hardness of heart.
The same Lord who commands forgiveness also calls His people to walk in truth.
And the same Christ who died for our sins rose again, demonstrating that death and darkness do not have the final word.
So no, you do not have to pretend that abuse is love.
You do not have to call fear peace.
You do not have to call silence submission.
You do not have to call manipulation leadership.
And you do not have to call the preservation of appearances the preservation of a godly marriage.
There may be grief ahead.
There may be difficult conversations.
There may be a long process of healing.
There may be decisions that require trusted pastoral guidance, professional help, and careful legal counsel.
But whatever happens next, remember where your ultimate hope belongs.
Not in a spouse becoming the person you hoped they would be.
Not in a church finally understanding your story.
Not in a marriage being restored on your preferred timetable.
Not even in the certainty of knowing how every chapter will unfold.
Your ultimate hope is in Jesus Christ.
The One who sees.
The One who knows.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who receives the brokenhearted.
The One who offers forgiveness through His blood and new life through His resurrection.
And the One who will never need a lie to defend His truth.
If you are in danger, seek safety.
If you are wounded, seek help.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you have harmed someone, accept accountability.
If you are walking alongside someone in crisis, listen carefully and protect their dignity.
And if you are struggling to believe that God still sees you, remember Hagar in the wilderness.
Remember the God who hears.
Remember the Savior who welcomes the weary.
Remember that the Gospel does not end with the grave.
Because this is the heart of our message.
Not because every marriage will be restored.
Not because every wound will disappear overnight.
Not because every earthly ending will match our expectations.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem what sin has shattered, restore dignity where shame has taken root, and lead His people into truth even through the darkest valleys.
And sometimes, the first evidence of that grace is not the return of the person who hurt you.
Sometimes it is the moment you finally understand that their cruelty was never the voice of God.
The God who sees your tears never asked you to mistake the hand that wounds you for the heart of the Savior who loves you.
